note.explanation: Meiosis makes four haploid cells from one diploid parent cell. In meiosis-I, homologous chromosomes separate; in meiosis-II, sister chromatids separate. For example, crossing over exchanges portions of non-sister chromatids, while non-disjunction can give gametes too many or too few chromosomes.
examples: Crossing over can produce new combinations of genes.
If chromosomes fail to separate properly, non-disjunction may produce gametes with an abnormal number of chromosomes.
note.simple: Meiosis is a two-division process that makes four cells, each with half the parent cell’s chromosome number.
note.title: Meiosis: making haploid cells
steps: In prophase-I, homologous chromosomes pair and crossing over can occur.
In anaphase-I, homologous chromosomes separate into two haploid sets.
At the end, four haploid daughter cells are formed.
note.answer: Meiosis produces four haploid daughter cells from one diploid parent cell.

written.text: How does crossing over contribute to genetic variation in meiosis?
written.finalAnswer: Crossing over creates new combinations of genes on chromosomes, so gametes carry unique sets of genes. This contributes to genetic diversity.

written.text: Describe the events that occur during the phases of meiosis-I.
written.finalAnswer: In prophase-I, homologous chromosomes pair, form tetrads and undergo crossing over. In metaphase-I, tetrads align at the equator. In anaphase-I, homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles. In telophase-I, nuclear envelopes reform, chromosomes uncoil and cytokinesis produces two haploid daughter cells.

modelAnswer: In prophase-I, chromatin condenses into chromosomes, and homologous chromosomes pair by synapsis to form tetrads.
Crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids, exchanging portions of chromosomes.
In metaphase-I, tetrads attached to spindle fibres align along the equator and form the metaphase plate.
In anaphase-I, homologous chromosomes separate; one chromosome from each pair moves toward each opposite pole. Each chromosome still contains two sister chromatids.
In telophase-I, spindles disappear, nuclear envelopes and nucleoli reform, and chromosomes uncoil into chromatin.
Cytokinesis occurs, producing two haploid daughter cells.

modelAnswer: In animals, meiosis produces gametes with half the number of chromosomes.
During sexual reproduction, male and female gametes join to make a zygote, restoring the original number of chromosomes.
In flowering plants, meiosis produces spores with half the number of chromosomes; the gametes produced by the new generation join to make a zygote with a full set.
Crossing over creates new combinations of genes on chromosomes, and each chromosome in the gametes carries a unique set of genes.
When diverse gametes combine, the zygote is genetically different from both parents, so meiosis contributes to genetic diversity.

steps.why: The division has four named phases, so first place them in the correct order.
steps.text: Meiosis-I consists of prophase-I, metaphase-I, anaphase-I and telophase-I.

steps.why: Pairing and exchange are the distinctive events to identify in prophase-I.
steps.text: In prophase-I, homologous chromosomes pair by synapsis to form tetrads, and crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids.

steps.why: The tetrads must line up before the homologous chromosomes can separate.
steps.text: In metaphase-I, tetrads attached to spindle fibres align along the equator.

steps.why: This is the reduction division: homologous chromosomes, not sister chromatids, separate.
steps.text: In anaphase-I, homologous chromosomes move toward opposite poles; each chromosome still contains two sister chromatids.

steps.why: Nuclear reformation and cytokinesis complete the first division.
steps.text: In telophase-I, nuclear envelopes reform, chromosomes uncoil, and cytokinesis produces two haploid daughter cells.

example.question: Describe the events that occur during the phases of meiosis-I.
example.answer: Meiosis-I pairs homologous chromosomes and allows crossing over, aligns tetrads at the equator, separates homologous chromosomes, and ends with two haploid daughter cells.

explain.title: What meiosis does
explain.body: It is the type of cell division in which each daughter cell receives half the number of chromosomes as compared to the parent cell. In meiosis, a diploid parent cell divides to produce four haploid daughter cells.

explain.title: Diploid and haploid
explain.body: Diploid means the cells in which chromosomes are in pairs (homologous pairs) while haploid means the cells with half number of chromosomes i.e., cells with no pairs of chromosomes.

explain.title: The first division
explain.body: In meiosis-I, the homologous chromosomes in a diploid cell separate and so two haploid daughter cells are produced. In prophase-I, homologous chromosomes pair, form tetrads and can exchange portions by crossing over.

explain.title: The second division
explain.body: Meiosis-II closely resembles mitosis. Sister chromatids separate during anaphase-II, and the process ends with four haploid daughter cells.

explain.title: Why meiosis matters
explain.body: Meiosis helps maintain chromosome number across generations and contributes to genetic diversity. Non-disjunction can make gametes with more or fewer chromosomes than normal.

mistakes: Do not say sister chromatids separate in anaphase-I; homologous chromosomes separate then, while sister chromatids separate in anaphase-II.
Do not confuse synapsis (pairing of homologous chromosomes) with crossing over (exchange of chromosome portions).
Do not say meiosis produces two daughter cells in total; meiosis-I produces two cells, and meiosis-II results in four.
Do not call the daughter cells diploid; they have half the parent cell’s chromosome number and are haploid.
When describing genetic diversity, explain that crossing over creates new gene combinations.
